newsitem.title: USA: Sled dog dies after first full day of Iditarod race.
newsitem.headline: Sled dog dies after first full day of Iditarod race.

text.p: A sled dog died early on Monday, the first day of competition in the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, but officials said the musher had been cleared of blame in a preliminary investigation.
The dog, on the team of Anchorage musher Bill Bass, collapsed just after leaving Skwentna, 149 miles (240 km) into the 1,161-mile (1,868 km) race route from Anchorage to Nome, officials said.
Bass returned to the checkpoint, where veterinarians examined the dead dog. Bass continued the race while officials await more detailed necropsy reports, said Mark Nordman, Iditarod race marshal.
Iditarod officials have ruled that any musher responsible for a dog's death will be thrown out of the race.
The Iditarod has never been run without a dog's death, and animal rights groups have protested the race because of this.
Meanwhile on Monday, top competitors streamed across the Alaska Range, the most mountainous part of the Iditarod trail.

Two-time champion Martin Buser held an edge over 1995 champion Doug Swingley late on Monday. Buser arrived at Rohn, 272 miles (438 km) into the course from Anchorage, at 5:02 p.m. (9:02 p.m. EST/0202 GMT on Tuesday) with all 16 of his starting dogs in harness. Swingley arrived there 36 minutes later, with 15 of his starting 16 dogs. Follwing him at 6:12 p.m. was Mitch Seavey of Seward, Alaska, with 14 dogs.
Mushers are allowed to start with as many as 16 dogs. They may drop dogs from the team as the animals tire, but may not add to the team during the race.
The past two champions reached the Nome finish line in nine days. The total race purse is over $400,000, of which the champion receives $50,000 and a new truck.
